extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate mathematics students writing proofs (homework and exams)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing rigorous, readable proofs for undergraduate mathematics homework and exams, emphasizing communication, notation, and logical structure. Covers conventions, anti-patterns, and presentation tips to help students write final proofs (not scratch work).

rubrics_metrics.name: The burden of communication lies on you, not on your reader
rubrics_metrics.description: It is your job to explain your thoughts; it is not your reader's job to guess them from a few hints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write to convince a skeptical reader with airtight logic and crystal clear language. If you didn't write something on the paper, you didn't communicate it; the grader will assume you didn't know it. Avoid leaving critical steps implicit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tell the reader what you're proving
rubrics_metrics.description: The statement you are proving should be on the same page as the beginning of your proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recopy the claim you are proving on homework (and ensure the statement is present on exams). This helps graders and helps you when reviewing later. Don't assume the reader remembers theorem numbers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use English words
rubrics_metrics.description: Use English sentences to connect equations and mathematical statements and display their logical relationships.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although equations appear, the proof should consist mostly of English words. Use phrases to explain transitions and the role of equations in the argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use complete sentences
rubrics_metrics.description: Use complete sentences, with verbs, to convey your logical train of thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While some complete sentences may be purely symbolic (e.g., a^3 = b^{-1}), avoid beginning sentences with symbols; prefer phrases like 'We see that...' to start sentences. Incomplete fragments impede clarity and communication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show the logical connections among your sentences
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicitly connect sentences using words/phrases that indicate logical relationships.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use connectors like 'Therefore', 'because', 'if... then...', 'if and only if' to indicate how one sentence follows from another and to make the logical flow explicit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know the difference between statements and objects
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish between mathematical objects (nouns) and statements (which are true or false).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be careful with clusters of symbols: determine if they denote an object (e.g., x^2 + 3) or a statement (e.g., x^2 + 3 < 7). A verb (like =, ≤, 'divides') indicates a statement. Misclassifying leads to logical and notational errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: "=" means equals
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't write A = B unless you mean that A actually equals B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid sloppy uses of '=' that conflate assumptions and consequences. Example anti-pattern: writing f(x) = x^2 = 2x when you mean 'if f(x)=x^2 then f'(x)=2x'. Use implication notation or words when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't interchange = and ⇒
rubrics_metrics.description: The equals sign connects objects; ⇒ (implies) connects statements. Avoid using ⇒ in formal write-ups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use '=' for equality of objects and written logical connectors or words for implication between statements (e.g., 'ab = a ⇒ b = 1' is a statement connecting statements). Prefer clear English.

rubrics_metrics.name: Say exactly what you mean
rubrics_metrics.description: Be precise in notation and language to avoid ambiguity (e.g., don't write A ∈ B when you mean A ⊆ B).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the precise mathematical notation available to express the intended relationship. Examples: distinguish membership vs. subset, and indicate when a_ij is an entry of matrix A versus element of set A.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't write anything unproven
rubrics_metrics.description: Every statement on your paper should be something you know to be true or clearly flagged as an assumption/claim/goal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you assert something not yet established, preface with 'assume', 'suppose', or 'if' (for temporary assumptions), or 'we need to show that', 'we claim that' (for goals). Otherwise the reader will think you've omitted part of the proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write strings of equalities (or inequalities) in the proper order
rubrics_metrics.description: When writing A = B ≤ C = D, the reader expects to see why each adjacent equality/inequality holds and that the intended point is A ≤ D.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Order equations so the progression is logically clear. Example: computing distance d: d = sqrt(12^2 + 5^2) = 13 shows Pythagorean step then arithmetic; avoid rearranged chains that obscure how a quantity was obtained (anti-patterns that confuse reader about which step proves what).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid circularity
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure that no step in your proof makes use of the conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume what you are trying to prove at any point in the argument. Working backwards is fine on scratch paper, but the written proof must start from hypotheses and proceed to the conclusion without circular arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't write the proof backwards
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not present work that starts with the conclusion and derives trivial truths; final proofs must begin with hypotheses and deduce the conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although working backwards can help discover a proof, the final write-up should proceed forward. Anti-pattern example: starting with the desired identity and deriving '1 = 1' only shows 'if conclusion then triviality', not a valid proof of the conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be concise
rubrics_metrics.description: Strive for proofs that are neither too short (omitting necessary steps) nor overly wordy (a long essay often signals lack of a proper proof).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most students err on brevity that hides logic; include necessary steps. Conversely, extremely long expositions may reflect mere intuition rather than a formal proof. A correct formal proof is often fairly short.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduce every symbol you use
rubrics_metrics.description: When you introduce a symbol (like k), make explicit what it stands for.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use clear phrases: 'Let n ∈ N', 'Let k be the least integer such that...', 'For every real number a...', 'Suppose X is a counterexample.' Avoid leaving symbols undefined or ambiguous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use appropriate quantifiers (once)
rubrics_metrics.description: When introducing a variable x ∈ S, make clear whether you mean 'for all x ∈ S' or 'there exists x ∈ S', and do not reintroduce the same variable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use phrases that indicate quantification: 'Let x ∈ S', 'for all x ∈ S', 'there exists x ∈ S', etc. Don't say 'where' to ambiguously introduce quantification. Introduce the quantifier once and avoid redefining the variable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a symbol to mean only one thing
rubrics_metrics.description: Once you assign a meaning to a symbol (e.g., x), its meaning is fixed for the duration of your proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not reuse the same symbol to mean different things in the same proof; this causes confusion. If you need a new object, introduce a new symbol.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't 'prove by example'
rubrics_metrics.description: You cannot prove a universal statement by providing examples; proofs must be logical arguments that cover all cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Providing one or many examples does not establish a claim that must hold 'for all' objects. Only valid uses of examples: counterexamples disproving a claim, or illustrative examples to help reader's understanding of a correct, general argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write 'Let x = ...', not 'Let ... = x'
rubrics_metrics.description: When giving an existing expression a new name, write 'Let new_symbol = old_expression' to make clear which symbol is new.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This convention indicates the new symbol is being defined. Writing the equality backwards ('Let a^2 = b') can confuse the reader about which symbol is new and which is being defined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make your counterexamples concrete and specific
rubrics_metrics.description: When providing a counterexample, make it fully explicit: name set elements or give a function rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not say vague phrases like 'θ could be one-to-one but not onto'; instead, exhibit an explicit function or set with named elements demonstrating the property. Counterexamples should be fully defined and concrete.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't include examples in proofs (except in limited cases)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples rarely add to a proof; only include them if they are counterexamples or are used to help understand complicated manipulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the logic is sound, examples are unnecessary. If the logic is flawed, examples won't fix it. Use examples only to disprove a claim or to illustrate how a general manipulation works for clarity, not as the substance of a proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use scratch paper
rubrics_metrics.description: Do messy exploration, false starts, and trial work on scratch paper; hand in only the final neat proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not submit scratch work. Only sentences that contribute to the proof should appear in the submitted write-up; avoid brain dumps. Find a real proof on scratch paper, then transcribe the final clear argument to clean paper.
